Linus
LY-nus
proper noun (a Roman believer)
Greek/Latin Linus; a believer at Rome who greeted Timothy with Paul (2 Timothy 4:21), traditionally reckoned an early leader of the Roman church.

📖 Biblical Definition

Linus was a believer at Rome who, with Eubulus, Pudens, Claudia, and the brethren, sent greeting to Timothy in the last chapter of Paul's final epistle. As with Pudens, Scripture tells us nothing more than his name and his presence among the faithful at Rome in the apostle's closing days. Early tradition reckons this Linus to be the same who served as a leading elder or “bishop” of the church at Rome after the apostles—and Rome later placed him in its list of popes as the immediate successor of Peter. The dictionary marks Linus chiefly as another of the obscure faithful whom God names and remembers, whose name is written in the Word and in the book of life, though not many wise or noble are called. But it also marks the abuse made of his name. The mere appearance of Linus as an early Roman elder, even if the tradition be granted, gives no warrant for the developed papal claims later read back upon him. That a faithful man led the church at Rome in the first century is no proof of a monarchical papacy or of Roman primacy over the universal church; the New Testament knows a plurality of elders in each congregation, not a single supreme bishop ruling all. The dictionary therefore honours Linus as a faithful saint and an early servant of the Roman church, while refusing the inference that his name validates the papal succession Rome built upon it. The truth of Linus is the simple, precious one of 2 Timothy 4:21: a brother who stood with Paul and whose name God has not forgotten.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A believer at Rome who greeted Timothy with Paul (2 Timothy 4:21), traditionally an early leader of the Roman church; honoured as an obscure faithful saint, while the papal-succession claims later built on his name are refused.

LINUS, proper noun. A believer at Rome in Paul's last days.

He greeted Timothy with Eubulus, Pudens, and Claudia (2 Timothy 4:21).

Tradition reckons him an early leading elder of the church at Rome.

Rome later listed him among its popes as Peter's successor.

Honoured as a faithful saint; the papal-succession claims on his name refused.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Ti 4:21 — "Do thy diligence to come before winter. Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren."

Php 4:3 — "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life."

1 Co 1:26 — "For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:"

Re 3:5 — "He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The abuse is the reading-back of developed papal-succession claims upon Linus's name, as though an early Roman elder proved a monarchical papacy and Roman primacy.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours Linus as another of the obscure faithful whom God names and remembers—a brother who stood with Paul at the end, whose name is written in the inspired Word and, by grace, in the Lamb's book of life. Not many wise or noble are called, yet God will not blot the faithful name out of His book but confess it before the Father. The simple, precious truth of 2 Timothy 4:21 is that a faithful man named Linus stood with the imprisoned apostle.

The corruption attaches to the use Rome has made of his name. Granting even the tradition that this Linus led the church at Rome after the apostles, the dictionary denies the inference built upon it: that an early Roman elder proves a monarchical papacy and the primacy of Rome over the universal church. The New Testament knows a plurality of elders in each congregation, not one supreme bishop ruling all; an early leading elder at Rome is no pope. The dictionary therefore honours Linus as a faithful early servant of the Roman church while refusing the papal-succession claims later read back upon him—for the validity of an office is the gospel preached, not a name on a list.
